props.title: Bulworth
props.initialSlug: Disillusioned senator goes rogue, drops truth bombs

sections.content: Bulworth (1998) stands as one of Hollywood's most daring political satires, with Warren Beatty directing and starring as a suicidal senator who starts rapping brutal truths about corporate corruption and racial inequality. The film's bold fusion of hip-hop culture with political commentary predates similar genre-bending works like Sorry to Bother You (2018) and Don't Look Up (2021). Beatty's unhinged performance captures the liberating madness of a politician who stops playing by the rules, creating a prescient commentary on media manipulation and political theater.

sections.content: The late 1990s marked a cynical turning point in political filmmaking. While All the President's Men (1976) portrayed journalists as noble truth-seekers, films like Wag the Dog (1997) and Primary Colors (1998) depicted politics as pure performance art. Bulworth stands out for combining this cynicism with genuine rage about economic inequality and racial injustice, themes that would become even more relevant in the decades following its release.

The film's mix of comedy and serious social commentary influenced later works like Vice (2018) and The Big Short (2015), which similarly use unconventional techniques to tackle complex political issues. Beatty's decision to have his character express himself through rap was revolutionary for 1998, anticipating how hip-hop would become a dominant force in political discourse and popular culture. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Political Satire

sections.content: Modern political comedies like The Death of Stalin (2017) and Don't Look Up (2021) follow Bulworth's template of using extreme situations to expose political absurdity. The film's influence can be seen in everything from Dave Chappelle's political comedy to Jordan Peele's social commentary in Get Out (2017), where entertainment and political messaging become inseparable.
